messages.body_plain:
Distance 3.5 users:

I have uploaded the following utility to the Distance web site
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/).  It can be downloaded from the
Distance Support, Updates and Extras page, under Downloads.

Enjoy!

 - Len Thomas

GxHisto: A macro for reproducing the detection function hisograms in MS Excel
Contributed by Dr. Tim Gerrodette, Southwest Fisheries Science Center, NMFS.

Distance 3.5 produces high-resolution plots of the detection function g(x)
(and probability density function f(x) for point transects).  These plots can
be copied and pasted into word processor packages (using Paste Special) as
pictures.  However, these pictures cannot then be edited or formatted.  This
macro allows you to recreate the plots from Distance within Microsoft Excel
as MS Charts.  These charts can then be reformatted as required.  In
addition, the macro can be edited to change the default chart format.

GxHisto is provided free of charge as a service to the Distance user
community.  If you have any comments about the macro, please contact Dr. Tim
Gerrodette at ti...@ucsd.edu.

messages.subject: Simulating Distance Data.
messages.body_plain:
I am teaching a field survey methods course in the Adirondack Mountains
later this summer and am interested in having students try distance
sampling on a series of stakes along a pre-determined transect.  I was
wondering if anyone has written a program that will give me the
perpendicular distances and appropriate intervals to simulate a known
density?  I'm guessing that such a program does not yet exist, so if I
don't hear from someone in a couple of days, I will finish the one I
have started!  Thanks in advance.

Brian Underwood

messages.subject: Re: Simulating Distance Data.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian (and others interested in field trials),

Probably the easiest thing for you is to write your own code, using any
programmable stats package.  You just need to generate numbers from a uniform
distribution for the along-trackline distances, and similarly for the
perpendicular distances.  (Beware the pseudo-random number generators in
programs like Excel - urban-computer-legend has it that they are quite bad!)

This will work well if you are going to have a large population of stakes (a
few hundred); however if you are going to have fewer than this you can refine
things a little to make sure that the distribution of stakes you end up with
(i.e. the realization of the pseudo-random process) is uniform in the
perpendicular direction.  To do this, divide up the perpendicular space into
bands and generate the same number of stakes in each band.  For example, if
you want to site 100 stakes at distances out to 25 meters then you could
divide the distances up into 10 bands of 5 meters (5 bands on each site of
the trackline) with 10 stakes sited "randomly" within in each band.

Another tip is to make sure that your population of stakes extends beyond
your transect strips.  If, for example, you have a transect that is 100
meters long, and you have an in-the-field truncation distance of 20 meters,
then place your stakes over an area extending 10 meters before and after the
line and out to 25 meters.  Some students will inevitably count some stakes
that are outside the stipulated strips, and this enables you to teach the
valuable lesson that these objects should be ignored (or at least flagged in
the data form as outside the study).

The king of wooden stake data is Jeff Laake (jeff....@noaa.gov), who did a
distance validation study for his masters in 1978.  He may be able to supply
some more tips.  I know of a few other field trials since then.  Mark Otto
and Ken Pollock used beer cans, and included cluster size (but not brand) as
an additional variable (Biometrics 46: 239-245).  David Anderson
(ande...@picea.cnr.colostate.edu), Ken Burnham, Bruce Lubow and myself, in
collaboration with Ron Marlow (Univ Nevada-Reno) and others organized a
survey of styrofoam moulds of desert tortoises, done by attendees at a
workshop on desert tortoise monitoring last year in Las Vegas.  Pseudo-
tortoise size and density were additional variables.  Also last year,
undergrads in our survey design course here at St Andrews did a survey for
golf tees (what else), where tee colour, height and cluster size were
additional variables.  If you're interested in the S-plus program used to
generate the locations, contact Miguel Bernal (mig...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk).

Perhaps others have additional tips or experience of field trials that they
can contribute?

If you do end up writing your own program, and feel that others would benefit
from it, feel free to send it to me with some instructions for its use, and
I'll post it on the Distance web site.

Good luck with your course,

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas (l...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk)
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

messages.subject: Power analysis of Z-test
messages.body_plain:
I have been using DISTANCE to calculate primate densities in a forest in
Uganda and I have used the Z-test (p381 in Buckland et al. 1993) to test
for differences between density estimates between two successive census
counts. I have been asked by one of the referees of one of my
manuscripts to calculate the power of this Z-test to detect a
difference.

I have looked at a couple of power analysis programs and both need a
sample size to calculate the power of a Z-test. What is the sample size
when I am using the density and standard errors calculated by DISTANCE
in the Z-test. Presumably it is  a function of the number of primate
groups seen and the number of transects? Can anyone help me with this?

Andy Plumptre

messages.subject: Announce: Distance web site update
messages.body_plain:
To Distance 3.5 users:

I have updated the Distance web site
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/) with an updated list of known
problems and workarounds.  Look on the Support, Updates and Extras page.

Most of the new problems are very minor.  However, we have discovered that
under some (seemingly rare) circumstances Distance fails to converge to the
maximum likelihood solution for hazard rate models and also fails to issue a
diagnostic warning message.  We are looking into this.

If you were experiencing the "Run time error 91" problem, please see the new
Known Problems list for a solution.

I also added a note under Downloads that the Excel macro for plotting the
detection function (GxHisto, by Dr Tim Gerrodette) only works in Excel 97 or
higher.  If you have an older version of Excel, contact the macro's author
(address is in the GxHisto readme).

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: Power analysis of Z-test
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 15 Jul 1999 08:11:14 -0400, Andy Plumptre wrote:

> >I have been using DISTANCE to calculate primate densities in a forest in
> >Uganda and I have used the Z-test (p381 in Buckland et al. 1993) to test
> >for differences between density estimates between two successive census
> >counts. I have been asked by one of the referees of one of my
> >manuscripts to calculate the power of this Z-test to detect a
> >difference.
> >
> >I have looked at a couple of power analysis programs and both need a
> >sample size to calculate the power of a Z-test. What is the sample size
> >when I am using the density and standard errors calculated by DISTANCE
> >in the Z-test. Presumably it is  a function of the number of primate
> >groups seen and the number of transects? Can anyone help me with this?
> >
> >Andy Plumptre
> >

Hi Andy,

You do not need the sample size if you are using a z-test.  Most power
analysis programs ask for the sample size because they want the standard
deviation as an input parameter and need to know n in order to convert this
to standard error.  In your case, you already have an estimate of standard
error - you worked it out in order to do your test - as sqrt[sqr (std err for
census 1) + sqr(std err for census 2)] (bottom line in the formula you cite).

In addition, for tests other than the z-test (t-test, F-test, chi-sq), you
need to know the degrees of freedom to calculate power - but not for the z-
test.

To do the calculation you're probably best off forgetting about power
programs and either programming it in a programmable stats package (SAS,
Splus, etc), or just working it out from a table of z values or probability
calculator program.  You can get the appropriate formula from most stat
books, but here it is for a two tailed test:

power = P(Z > Z_(alpha/2) - (mu_0-mu_1)/sigma) +
        P(Z < -Z_(alpha/2) - (mu_0-mu_1)/sigma)

P(Z > x) is the probability of a random value of Z being greater than x
    (get this from the tables at the back of a stat book)
Z_(alpha/2) is the critical value of a z distribution at alpha_2
    (eg 1.96 at alpha = 0.05)
mu_0 is the value for difference in density under the null hypothesis
    (probably 0)
mu_1 is the value for difference in density under the alternative hypothesis
sigma is the standard error (standard deviation of the difference in
estimates - see my first paragraph)

In SAS, the commands are something like

ALPHA = 0.15; *Put your own alpha in here;
MU0 = 0; *Put your own null hypothesis here - probably 0;
MU1 = 1; *Put your own alternative hypothesis here;
SIGMA = 0.5; * Put your own SE here;
ZC_UP = PROBIT(1-ALPHA/2);
ZC_LO = -ZC_UP;
EFFSIZ = (MU0-MU1)/SIGMA;
POWER = 1 - PROBNORM(ZC_UP - EFFSIZ) + PROBNORM(ZC_LO - EFFSIZ);

I don't have a copy of SAS here, so can't check if the code works or not, but
hopefully it will!

A few caveats:

- its up to you to decide what a biologically important alternative
hypothesis should be.  Don't use the estimated difference in densities from
your test! (see Thomas, 1997, Cons. Biol. 11: 276-280 if you're not sure why
this is.)

- the above formulation assumes that the estimates of density at the two
times are statistically independent.  If, for example, you used a pooled f(0)
then you'll need to modify the calculation for the standard error of the
difference (although you'll presumably already have done this for your test).
An example of how to go about calculating variance when components of
estimation are in common is in the Distance Sampling book, starting at page
380.

- I'm not really very keen on hypothesis testing in general.  I'd say it is
more informative to estimate the difference in density between census periods
and then put a confidence interval about the difference.  This way you give
all the information about the possible biological importance of the result
and your uncertainty in the estimates, rather than having to resort to the
tortuous mental back-flips involved in justifying a retrospective power
analysis.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas (l...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk)
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

and SIZETRAN. The following references may be useful:

Karanth K. U. 1991. Line transect method for censusing elephants in
Nagarahole. Pages 51-52 in Censusing elephants in forests (Editors: U.
Ramakrishnan, J. A. Santhosh and R. Sukumar). Asian Elephant
Conservation Centre, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, India.

Karanth K. U. and Sunquist M. E. 1992.  Population structure, density
and biomass of large herbivores in the tropical forests of Nagarahole,
India.  Journal of Tropical Ecology 8: 21-35.

Karanth K. U. and Sunquist M. E.  1995.  Prey selection by tiger,
leopard and dhole in tropical forests. Journal of Animal Ecology 64:
439-450.

Karanth K. U. and Nichols J. D. 1998.  Estimating tiger densities in
India from camera trap data using photographic captures and recaptures.
Ecology Vol 79 (8): 2852-2862.

Karanth K. U.  Estimation of large mammal densities using line transect
sampling: a case study from Nagarahole National Park.  In Proceedings of
the Workshop on Field Research Methods. Eds. A. J. T. Johnsingh, S. P.
Goyal, P. K. Mathur, S. Choudhury and P. Krausman. Wildlife Institute of
India, Dehra Dun, India (In Press).

Karanth K. U. and Stith B. M. 1999. Prey depletion as a critical
determinant of tiger population viability. In Riding the Tiger: Tiger
conservation in human dominated landscapes (Editors: J. Seidensticker,
S. Christie and P. Jackson), Cambridge University Press.

I hope you will find some of these useful.  All the best,
KARANTH

messages.subject: Naturalist Italian student -Reply
messages.body_plain:
Hello Graziella:

The Wyoming Game and Fish Department is using aerial line transect sampling to estimate abundance of pronghorn in most management units (i.e., populations) across the state. Our application of distance sampling may not be directly comparable to terrestrial surveys of ungulates in forested habitats because pronghorn occupy open habitats and are relatively amenable to aerial surveys.

We started using our technique for pronghorn management in the late 1980's when TRANSECT was the analysis program and have worked up through the various versions of Distance. We just started using the newest Windows version, Distance 3.5, release 5.

We conduct surveys from fixed-wing aircraft where the wing struts and windows have been specifically marked to denote prescribed perpendicular ground distance intervals when the plane is flown at the appropriate height. Onboard computers capture the actual height of the plane above ground level using radar (or laser) altimeters in order to adjust distance bands for the actual height above ground level.  Some fairly strict procedures are required to address the assumptions of the technique. To some degree, the protocol we use constrains the type of analyses we perform using Distance. The analysis we run is for clustered populations using perpendicular distances grouped into intervals. We prepared a manual that describes our procedures and basic analyses using Distance 2.2.

For terrestrial surveys, there are other options for obtaining accurate distance data (e.g., laser rangefinders) than the approach we use. Please let me know if I can answer any other questions regarding our use of distance sampling and analysis using Distance.

Good luck!
Rich Guenzel
Wildlife Biologist
Wyoming Game and Fish Dept.
528 S. Adams
Laramie, WY 82070 USA
